blocks.text: This is tolerable, and not to be compared with the absurdities of the masters in the Talmudic tractate Ioma, ch. 8, fol. 75 b, where, by the definition of Rabbi Chanina Barabba, ד׳ מיני סליו הן ואלו הן שיכלי וקיכלי ופסיוני ושליו מעליא דכולהו שיכלי גריעי דכולהו שליו, There are four kinds of quails, namely sicli (that is, συκαλὶς [sykalis], ficedula [fig-pecker]), and kichli (that is, κίχλη [kichlē], turdus [thrush]), and phisioni (φασιανὸς [phasianos], phasianus [pheasant]), and selau (the quail properly so called); of which the most excellent is sicli (the fig-pecker), and the meanest of all selau (the quail properly so called). Hence it is that some interpreters render שלו or שלוים as פסיונין, that is, pheasants. So Jonathan on Exod. XVI, 13: וסליקו פסיינין וחפו ית משריתא, And pheasants came up and covered the camp. And R. Joseph the Blind on Psal. CV, 40: שאלו בסרא ואיתי פסיונין, They asked for meat, and he brought pheasants: evidently, for men born for the belly and the gullet it is not enough that God granted quails to the fathers with a liberal hand; so they chose to add those birds that most delight the palate: fig-peckers, thrushes and pheasants. Among these the fig-pecker leads the line,
The waxen fig-pecker that gleams with its broad loin
in Martial, book 5. Hence Juvenal, Satire 14:
— — — who, from a spendthrift father, learned to scrape truffles, to season a mushroom, and to drown fig-peckers swimming in the same sauce.

It was peculiar to the fig-pecker that gluttons liked the whole of it, not, as with other birds, the rump alone. Gellius, book 15, ch. 8, from Favorinus: The masters of the cookshop and of luxury, etc., deny that any bird except the fig-pecker ought to be eaten whole. [II, 653] Of other birds and fattened fowls, unless so much is served that the guests are filled from the rump and the lower part, they think the banquet mean through scarcity; and that those who eat the upper part of birds and fowls have no palate. Hence Martial, book 3, Epigram 59:
A golden turtle-dove fills you with its huge rump.
And Epigram 81:
And gives the turtle-doves' rumps to his concubine.

After the fig-pecker follows קיכלי, κίχλη [kichlē], the thrush; these birds are often joined as equal, or nearly equal, delicacies. Cornelius Celsus, book 2, ch. 18: Of the birds that rely on flight, the larger give firmer nourishment than the small, such as fig-peckers and the thrush. Suetonius, Tiberius, ch. 42: He gave Asellius Sabinus two hundred thousand sesterces for a dialogue in which he had staged a contest of the mushroom, the fig-pecker, the oyster and the thrush. Plautus in the Captivi, alluding to both birds:
There is need of the Turdetani, need of the Ficedulenses,

But, contrary to the opinion of the Hebrews, those who measure everything by the delights of the palate give first place to the fat thrush. The Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Peace: Αἱ κίχλαι εἶδος στρουθῶν, δοκοῦσι δὲ πρὸς τρυφὴν ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν περισπούδαστοι εἶναι μᾶλλον· [Hai kichlai eidos strouthōn, dokousi de pros tryphēn ek tōn allōn ptēnōn perispoudastoi einai mallon] Thrushes are a kind of small bird which are sought out above others for delicacies. Horace, book 1, Epist. 15:
He used to say that those who devour their goods are right, since nothing is better than a fat [col. 95] thrush. — — — —
Martial, Xenium 92:
Among birds the thrush, if anyone contends with me as judge, among quadrupeds the hare holds the first glory.
And elsewhere:
Perhaps you like a crown woven of roses or rich nard, but I like a crown made of thrushes.
And again:
There a crown heavy with fat thrushes.
Persius, Satire 6:
Nor skilled to know the delicate savour of thrushes.

That is, not a gourmand, a λίχνος [lichnos], who knows well what flavour thrushes have. So formerly at Athens, when discipline was stricter, the young ^{a)} were not permitted ὀψοφαγεῖν [opsophagein], [II, 654] οὐδὲ κιχλίζειν [oude kichlizein], to eat fish, nor thrushes, that is, to dine delicately. And Pompey, when ill, refused to have a thrush sought from Lucullus, although the physician ordered it, using this famous saying: Οὐκοῦν, εἰ μὴ Λούκουλλος ἐτρύφα, Πομπήϊος οὐκ ἂν ἔζησεν; [Oukoun, ei mē Loukoullos etrypha, Pompēios ouk an ezēsen?] Would Pompey then not live without the luxury of Lucullus? This so pleased Plutarch that he related it at least four times: in the Lucullus, in the Pompey, in the Apophthegmata, and in the book Whether an old man should engage in public affairs.
